summary: Customer wants to scope a 3-4 week POC to validate performance & cost for a document summarization workflow. Core objectives: integrate customer scripts into Redwood benchmark harness, run both streaming and non-streaming load tests, measure time-to-first-token and end-to-end latency (p50/p95), validate resource sizing for Dedicated vs Hosted, and confirm security posture for Private deployment if needed.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-29
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO, DataHarbor), Liam O'Connor (ML Eng), Priya Singh (SRE), Ethan Wu (Product), Nina Roberts (Procurement)

AUTO SUMMARY (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- DataHarbor is evaluating a POC to validate inferencing economics and latency for a large-batch document summarization use case. They want Redwood's benchmark harness to run their customer scripts and compare streaming vs non-streaming performance.
- Main success criteria: p95 latency under 1.2s for short summaries (<=128 tokens) and cost-per-1k-requests target.
- Proposed pilot: 3-4 weeks including integration, synthetic load testing, and a small production shadow run.

--- Transcript Body ---
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Avery Chen from Redwood, Diego our SE.
[00:06] Maya Patel: Hi, Maya here, CTO at DataHarbor.
[00:08] Liam O'Connor: Liam, ML eng.
[00:09] Priya Singh: Priya, SRE.
[00:10] Ethan Wu: Ethan, product.
[00:11] Nina Roberts: Nina, procurement.
[00:12] Diego Morales: Thanks folks. Goal for today is to scope the benchmark plan and how your existing scripts integrate. We'll cover streaming vs non-streaming load shapes and success criteria.

[00:35] Maya Patel: Thanks. Quick background: we run a doc summarization pipeline — daily batch of ~200k docs, but real-time summarization for web requests is about 1.5k qps peak across regions. For the POC we just want to prove we can meet latency targets and get a cost estimate.

[01:05] Avery Chen: Helpful. What are your latency SLOs and how important is time-to-first-token (TTFT) vs total completion time?

[01:14] Liam O'Connor: For UI use-cases TTFT matters a lot — users see a spinner, so if streaming gives a first token under 300ms it's huge. Our p95 end-to-end target for 128-token summaries is 1.2s.

[01:29] Priya Singh: And on the infra side we need to know the concurrency and how sessions map to KV cache usage — stateful sessions vs stateless short summaries.

[01:42] Diego Morales: Great. For the harness integration we typically accept a couple of forms: we can run your exact Python script (you provide a lightweight wrapper) inside our benchmark harness, or you can point our harness at a service endpoint and we'll replay requests. For streaming tests we need a streaming client that can report TTFT and chunk latencies — k6 has streaming constraints, so we sometimes use a custom locust or their async harness.

[02:10] Maya Patel: We have custom Python scripts that talk to our frontend and call the model via an internal service. Would it be easier to paste those scripts or to provide an API stub?

[02:21] Diego Morales: Either works. Ideally you give us a sanitized script that we can run in a container. If it requires auth or internal dependencies, provide a stub that replicates the request/response shape. We'll provide a sample wrapper.

[02:35] Avery Chen: Also want to flag model selection — are you planning to use an open LLM or our curated variant? Model size/quantization will affect throughput.

[02:45] Liam O'Connor: We're experimenting with two model families: a 7B quantized variant for cost-sensitive paths and a 13B for higher quality. We'll likely benchmark both.

[02:56] Diego Morales: Perfect. We'll include both as separate scenarios, and measure tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency, and cost estimate per 1k requests.

[03:10] Ethan Wu: On streaming vs non-streaming — can you explain the differences in what you measure?

[03:17] Diego Morales: Sure. Non-streaming test measures time from request start to final token emitted. Streaming measures time-to-first-token (TTFT), inter-chunk latencies, and time to last token. Streaming is more realistic for UI, but it's more sensitive to network jitter and the client's ability to process chunks. Load generation also changes — we need clients that can maintain many concurrent open streams.

[03:45] Priya Singh: That means our SRE team needs to make sure firewall/NAT timeouts can handle long-lived SSEs or websockets. We'll confirm.

[03:55] Maya Patel: In terms of success criteria beyond raw latency, we also want to see model hallucination/quality regressions. Can we run a small eval set for quality checks?

[04:07] Diego Morales: Absolutely. We recommend a held-out evaluation prompt set (1000 examples) that we run and compute ROUGE/BLEU and also human spot checks. For the POC we'll include a qualitative check to ensure the cheaper 7B quantized model doesn't drop below your threshold.

[04:25] Liam O'Connor: Good. How do you compute cost? Are you doing per-token for Hosted and different for Dedicated?

[04:31] Avery Chen: We'll produce a cost model: hosted per-token estimate and an amortized cost for dedicated GPU capacity based on utilization. For Dedicated we show unit economics at different utilization levels.

[04:45] Maya Patel: Timeline — what does integration look like? We want lucidity on the weeks.

[04:50] Diego Morales: Typical POC: week 0 — integration and harness setup (get scripts running), week 1 — baseline non-streaming tests, week 2 — streaming tests + additional model variants, week 3 — cost analysis and shadow traffic run, with buffer for follow-ups. So 3-4 weeks.

[05:10] Maya Patel: That aligns with our expectations. Procurement might need SOC2 before we move to dedicated.

[05:16] Nina Roberts: Yes, procurement will want SOC2 Type II reports, data residency notes, and a draft SOW.

[05:22] Avery Chen: We'll share SOC2 docs and a standard SOW template. We'll also include an example runbook for the benchmark harness.

[05:30] Priya Singh: About the harness — what load tools are supported? We use k6 for API tests; for streaming we've used custom locust + async clients.

[05:39] Diego Morales: We support k6 for non-streaming and recommend Locust or our async runner for streaming. We also have sample k6 scripts that simulate multiple prompt sizes. For Customer scripts, containerizing them as a lightweight package is easiest.

[05:55] Liam O'Connor: For the streaming tests, we need the harness to capture first-byte times from the server, not just the client SDK timestamp which can be noisy.

[06:05] Diego Morales: We'll instrument with server-side tracing hooks if you want deeper insight; otherwise client-measured TTFT is fine for acceptance tests. If you're doing Dedicated or Private, we can enable tracing and token-level logs in a safe way.

[06:20] Ethan Wu: Any gotchas around KV-cache or re-use? Our production flow re-uses context for a subset of users.

[06:27] Diego Morales: Yes — if you have session affinity and KV cache hits, throughput improves. For benchmarks we should include two profiles: cold (no cache) and hot (cache warmed). That gives you realistic delta.

[06:40] Maya Patel: Let's be conservative — include 70/30 split hot/cold in our load plan.

[06:47] Diego Morales: Noted. Also what concurrency numbers do you want? You mentioned 1.5k qps at peak, is that global or per-region?

[06:55] Maya Patel: Global. For a single region we'd expect up to 400 qps. So our test matrix should include 100, 400, and 1k RPS scenarios to stress different configs.

[07:10] Priya Singh: We'll need to lock a 2-hour maintenance window to open a VPC peering route for the private tests. I'll coordinate.

[07:18] Avery Chen: Perfect. For data handling — if you're sending customer text, please sanitize PII. We support KMS for encryption and can do private deployments if necessary.

[07:28] Maya Patel: We'll sanitize test data for now, but may need Private later. We'll share requirements.

[07:34] Diego Morales: On measurement artifacts we'll deliver CSVs with per-request latencies, token counts, and a cost estimate spreadsheet. We'll also attach traces for any p95 anomalies.

[07:45] Liam O'Connor: Can you also produce per-model throughput graphs and a recommended GPU sizing?

[07:50] Diego Morales: Yes — we'll include tokens/sec per-GPU and an estimated fleet size for your target utilization.

[08:00] Nina Roberts: For contracting, what's the minimal commitment for Dedicated? Procurement wants numbers to evaluate budgeting.

[08:06] Avery Chen: We can do a short term reserved capacity or a proof-of-concept monthly seat. For the POC we'll stick to hosted or a short-term Dedicated trial. We'll follow up with exact numbers in the pricing doc.

[08:18] Maya Patel: Any risk about streaming tests causing clients to drop because of NAT ephemeral ports?

[08:23] Priya Singh: That's on us to validate, we'll check NAT table settings.

[08:28] Diego Morales: We'll provide recommended client concurrency and socket settings in the runbook.

[08:35] Ethan Wu: For quality measurements, can you run automatic similarity metrics plus a small human eval panel?

[08:41] Diego Morales: Yep, we can run ROUGE and also help coordinate a small 10-person annotation pass if you want a human quality signal. That may extend timeline by a few days.

[08:55] Maya Patel: We're ok with a small human spot-check. Focus is on latency + cost first.

[09:03] Avery Chen: Okay to recap and assign owners.

[09:10] Avery Chen: Action items: Avery shares harness repo and sample scripts; Diego drafts load plan; Liam provides prompt set and SLOs; Priya confirms network window; procurement gets SOC2 docs.

[09:30] Maya Patel: Sounds good. We'll aim to have materials to you early next week.

[09:36] Nina Roberts: We'll expect SOC2 and SOW for review.

[09:40] Avery Chen: We'll shoot all that over by tomorrow EOD. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the test window.

[09:48] End of call

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap at ~03:00 and some proper nouns (model names) may be garbled.
